newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian court wipes out state tax rights.
newsitem.headline: Australian court wipes out state tax rights.

text.p: Australia's highest court on Tuesday struck out state rights to tax alcohol, tobacco and petrol, threatening to wipe out billions of dollars of revenue.
In a four to three majority ruling, the High Court of Australia ruled that business franchise fees were in fact an excise, which only the national government can raise under Australia's constitution.
"We are conscious that this judgment has the most serious implications for the revenues of the states and territories," said the four majority judges, including chief judge Gerard Brennan.
"It is clear that it's a big loss for the states," lawyer George Williams told reporters outside the court.

"The states, in order to maintain their approximately A$5.0 billion (US$3.7 billion) of revenue base will need to turn to the Commonwealth," said Williams, an Australian National University constitutional expert.

Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters the national government would pass legislation to levy its own taxes to replace the state charges, which account for about 16 percent of the income raised by Australia's six states and two territories.
The national, state and territory governments on Tuesday were negotiating how to replace the newly outlawed levies and how to share the income from a new system.
The court ruling is the second blow to state finances in two days. Costello on Monday closed a loophole that allowed states to boost prices for asset sales by helping buyers cut their tax.
Tuesday's judgment, on a challenge by two tobacco retailers, only applies specifically to tobacco franchise fees in New South Wales state, but will flow on to other states and charges.
"What this judgment does is it confirms the trend, particularly since 1949, that the states are really kept out of the area of raising revenue from indirect taxes on goods," Williams said.

The ruling is likely to see prices for petrol, alcohol and tobacco rise at first in some states, because the national government cannot levy different rates in different areas and is expected to set its rates at the highest existing levels.
Currently, the franchise fees vary between states and one, Queensland, has no charge at all on petrol.

But Costello said Canberra's help was conditional on consumers paying no more -- flagging the possibility of a rebate in some states -- and on the new charges being clearly identified as collections for the states.
"We will not be party to anything that puts up prices," Costello said.
Acting Labor opposition leader Gareth Evans indicated the opposition would support federal legislation to replace the state excises, if the rescue package was fair.
Business groups said the decision offered a prime opportunity to overhaul the outdated and uneven tax system.
"Fundamental tax reform must be an inevitable consequence of the High Court's decision," said Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Mark Paterson.
The states must immediately stop collecting the levy. But Canberra can legislate to legalise past collections and to prevent retailers and wholesalers claiming compensation.
The states and territories already rely on Canberra for half their income, divided up at a traditionally acrimonious annual summit of state, territory and national leaders.
